content: The Allerød Oscillation, also known as the Allerød Chronozone, occurred approximately 11,800 to 11,000 years ago. This period marked a significant climatic warming phase during the late Pleistocene epoch, preceding the abrupt cooling of the Younger Dryas. Arizona is geographically located at 34°N latitude and 112°W longitude. The Younger Dryas Boundary (YDB) markers, which include magnetic grains, microspherules, iridium, soot, and fullerenes containing extraterrestrial helium, are found in sediment layers just beneath the black mat layer. This black mat represents a lithological break that coincides with the end of the Clovis period, prior to the formation of the black mat itself. At Murray Springs, Clovis artifacts, a fire pit, and the nearly complete skeleton of an adult mammoth were discovered, all of which were covered by the black mat layer. Excavations led by Vance Haynes Jr. and colleagues also uncovered hundreds of mammoth footprints preserved in sand, which were later infilled by black mat sediments. These footprints and the mammoth skeleton appear to have been rapidly buried following the Younger Dryas Boundary event. No in situ Clovis points or remains of extinct megafauna have been recovered from within or above the black mat layer, suggesting that both the mammoths and Clovis hunting technology disappeared simultaneously, except in isolated cases. The end-Clovis stratum, corresponding to the Younger Dryas Boundary, is well-dated at Murray Springs, Arizona, with radiocarbon dates averaging 10,890 years before present (calibrated to approximately 12,920 calendar years ago). Similarly, the nearby Lehner site has radiocarbon dates averaging 10,940 years before present (calibrated to approximately 12,930 calendar years ago). Haynes correlated the base of the black mat with the onset of Younger Dryas cooling, dated to approximately 12,900 years ago in the Greenland GISP2 ice core. Wisconsin is geographically located at 44.5°N latitude and 89.5°W longitude. During the Allerød period, the region experienced the Two Creeks Interval, a late Pleistocene interstadial. The Two Creeks Buried Forest provides a precise record of glacial advances and retreats during the Wisconsinan glaciation. Following the retreat of the Cary glacier, a boreal-like forest of black and white spruce, hemlock, pine, mosses, and other plants developed in the Two Creeks area near Lake Michigan. However, the advancing Valders glacier later flooded the forest, covering it with silt and clay, which preserved the forest by preventing decomposition. Subsequent glacial activity flattened the forest, leaving behind additional clay layers embedded with logs and debris. The black mat layer, a carbon-rich stratum dating to approximately 12,900 years ago, has been identified at around 50 Clovis-age sites across North America. This layer is contemporaneous with the onset of Younger Dryas cooling. Extinct Pleistocene megafauna bones and Clovis tool assemblages are found below this black layer but not within or above it, indicating a significant ecological and cultural shift. The causes of these extinctions, Younger Dryas cooling, and the termination of the Clovis culture remain controversial. Evidence suggests an extraterrestrial impact event around 12,900 years ago, which may have triggered abrupt environmental changes, contributing to Younger Dryas cooling, widespread extinctions, and rapid shifts in human behavior. Clovis-age sites in North America are overlain by a thin, discrete layer containing varying abundances of magnetic grains with iridium, magnetic microspherules, charcoal, soot, carbon spherules, glass-like carbon containing nanodiamonds, and fullerenes with extraterrestrial helium. These markers are consistent with an extraterrestrial impact and associated biomass burning around 12,900 years ago. This layer extends across at least 15 Carolina Bays, which are elliptical depressions oriented northwest across the Atlantic Coastal Plain. The Younger Dryas black layers, or black mats, are dark gray to black due to increased organic carbon content (0.05–8%) compared to surrounding strata. These layers represent relatively moist conditions with higher water tables, as indicated by the presence of mollisols, wet-meadow soils, algal mats, or pond sediments. In some cases, these deposits include dark gray to black diatomites. However, not all sites exhibit a black layer; some contain white to gray diatomaceous strata of Younger Dryas age due to limited groundwater interaction. Nanodiamonds, which are produced during extraterrestrial collisions, have been identified in the Younger Dryas Boundary layer, dating to approximately 12,800 calendar years ago. These nanodiamonds are also found at the Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary, 65 million years ago, which is associated with mass extinctions. The distribution of nanodiamonds across 50 million square kilometers of the Northern Hemisphere supports the hypothesis of an extraterrestrial impact event during the Younger Dryas. The Laacher See volcanic eruption in present-day Germany occurred around 12,880 years ago, coinciding with the onset of North Atlantic cooling and the Younger Dryas. This eruption, with a Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) of 6, released over 20 cubic kilometers of tephra and significant amounts of sulfur into the atmosphere, potentially triggering long-term climate feedback mechanisms involving sea ice and oceanic circulation. This event may have contributed to the cascade of climate shifts observed during the Younger Dryas. Mount Kilimanjaro, located at 3°4'33S and 37°21'12E, provides a Holocene climate record through its ice cores. These cores reveal periods of abrupt climate change, including events approximately 8,300, 5,200, and 4,000 years ago. The latter coincides with the First Dark Age, a period of severe drought in tropical Africa.
